title: Zuriel Original-Language Word Study Collection — Batch 1
description: Context-sensitive Hebrew, Greek and Aramaic word-study cards. These are study aids, not a substitute for verse-level parsing or critical lexicons.
editorialPolicy: Transliterations and glosses are concise aids; check the actual form and syntax in each passage.
No Strong's identifiers, morphology, pronunciation audio or exhaustive semantic claims are supplied unless separately verified.
Do not derive theology from etymology alone; context governs meaning.
Respect Jewish reading conventions for the divine name.

entries.contextualGloss: Wind, breath or spirit. In Genesis 1:2 the term describes the divine presence moving over the waters, with translation discussions about 'Spirit of God' or 'wind from God'. In Ezekiel 37:1-14 the vision deliberately moves through wind, breath and spirit imagery as the bones receive life; the passage interprets the vision as Israel's restoration. Psalm 51:10-12 asks for inner renewal and the sustaining presence of God's Holy Spirit.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The word can denote wind, breath or spirit. Do not assume every occurrence names the Holy Spirit; grammar, collocation and literary context determine the sense.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult a critical lexicon and the specific verse for parsing.

entries.contextualGloss: Glory, honour or weight; it can describe God's revealed majesty or the honour and significance accorded to people.

entries.contextualGloss: Word, message, statement, account or reason. In John 1:1-18 the Logos is present in the beginning, related to God, involved in creation and identified with Jesus' embodied life in verse 14. Hebrews 4:12 uses 'word of God' in a different context for the living, active word that exposes the heart; do not transfer every detail of John's title into every occurrence.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Logos has a broad Greek range. John 1 gives it a distinctive theological role, but not every New Testament occurrence means the personal title 'the Word'.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: grace, favour or gracious gift
entries.interpretiveCaution: Grace has a range of uses; distinguish divine saving grace from ordinary favour by context.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Repentance: a changed mind and reorientation expressed in turning. Mark 1:14-15 places the call to repent within Jesus' announcement of God's kingdom. Acts 2:37-38 connects repentance to the hearers' response to Jesus. 2 Corinthians 7:9-10 distinguishes godly grief that produces repentance from worldly grief; sorrow alone is not the same as changed direction.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not reduce repentance to feeling guilty or to a word-origin formula. Read the response and its fruits in each passage; never use repentance language to pressure victims to remain in harm.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not restrict every occurrence to one church office; the context identifies the kind of service.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: helper, advocate or one called alongside to assist

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Kingdom, reign or royal rule; in Jesus' teaching it often refers to God's reign and the life shaped by its arrival.

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Life or living; the Hebrew plural form can express life as a whole, lived vitality and the flourishing set before God's people.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The plural form commonly expresses life; do not infer a separate doctrine from grammatical number alone.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: clan, family group or kinship household
entries.interpretiveCaution: The social unit may extend beyond a modern nuclear family; read the historical kinship setting carefully.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: work, labour or service; in some contexts service rendered in worship

entries.contextualGloss: kinsman-redeemer or one who acts as a family redeemer or advocate
entries.interpretiveCaution: The legal and family role in Torah and Ruth should not be collapsed into every later theological use of redemption.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty or faithful kindness. In Exodus 34:6 it appears with compassion, grace, patience and faithfulness in God's self-description. Psalm 136 repeats the enduring-love refrain while recalling creation and deliverance. Hosea 6:6 contrasts steadfast love and knowledge of God with empty ritual.
entries.interpretiveCaution: No single English word captures every occurrence. Do not reduce hesed to sentiment or assume every use describes a formal covenant formula.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Goodness, uprightness or moral excellence. In Galatians 5:22-23 it appears among the fruit of the Spirit; Romans 15:14 describes believers as filled with goodness and knowledge; Ephesians 5:9 links goodness with the fruit of light.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not treat goodness as mere niceness or as a way to earn salvation; these passages describe Spirit-shaped character expressed in life.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Living being, life, person, self or desire according to context. Genesis 2:7 calls the formed human a living nephesh; it describes the whole living person rather than plainly teaching that a detachable soul was inserted into a body. Leviticus 17:11 closely associates nephesh with life and blood. Psalm 42:1-2 uses it for the worshipper's own self, which thirsts for God.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Avoid importing a later philosophical definition of soul into every occurrence. Hebrew usage includes the person, life and appetite, depending on context.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew or Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Good, beneficial, pleasing or well-being. Genesis 1 uses the term in the repeated evaluation of creation; Psalm 34:8 invites people to taste and see the Lord's goodness; Micah 6:8 describes what is good in a call to justice, mercy and humility.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The adjective's sense depends on its subject and setting; do not make every occurrence mean moral perfection or a guaranteed pleasant outcome.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Hebrew form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Proclamation or announced message. 1 Corinthians 1:21 contrasts the proclamation with worldly expectations of wisdom; Romans 16:25 speaks of the proclamation of Jesus Christ; 2 Timothy 4:17 describes Paul being enabled to fully proclaim the message.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The noun refers to proclamation or the message proclaimed; it does not automatically encode every element of a complete theology of the Gospel in every context.
entries.morphologyStatus: Not asserted; consult the specific Greek form, syntax and a critical lexicon before assigning morphology.

entries.contextualGloss: Righteousness or justice; depending on context it can describe God's saving faithfulness, a right standing before God, or conduct shaped by what is right.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not assume the term has only a forensic or only an ethical sense; follow the argument and its grammatical setting in each passage.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: To bow down, do obeisance or worship; the action may express reverence toward God or homage toward a person, as the immediate context shows.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not reduce every occurrence to one physical posture or infer the full theology of worship from the verb alone.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: To serve or render religious service; New Testament contexts connect the verb with service offered to God, worship and devoted allegiance.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Distinguish this term from broader words for service by reading the object and setting of each occurrence.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Spirit, breath or wind; it may refer to the Holy Spirit, the human spirit or wind, and context must determine the referent.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The same Greek word has several referents; do not assume every occurrence means the Holy Spirit.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Presence, arrival or coming; in several New Testament passages it describes the awaited coming of Christ, while its basic sense is established by context.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Interpret each occurrence in its literary setting and avoid building detailed end-times chronology from the noun alone.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: From above, from the beginning or again; John's use in the conversation with Nicodemus carries a deliberate ambiguity that the dialogue develops.
entries.interpretiveCaution: In John 3, preserve the wordplay between 'from above' and 'again' rather than flattening the conversation to only one English gloss.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: To be moved with compassion; Gospel narratives use it for deep concern that issues in merciful action toward people in need.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not treat compassion as sentiment alone; observe the concrete response that follows in each narrative.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Help or helper; the word can describe assistance and is also used of God as the help of His people, so it does not inherently imply inferiority.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not derive a hierarchy of worth or authority from this noun alone; attend to its varied biblical uses and the whole creation narrative.

entries.contextualGloss: To redeem, act as a kinsman-redeemer or reclaim; in legal and narrative settings it can describe restoring family land, freedom or a relative's standing.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The kinsman-redeemer institution belongs to specific Israelite social and legal settings; explain those settings before applying the imagery to Christ.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Wisdom or skill; biblical usage includes practical competence, moral discernment and reverent living shaped by God's instruction.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Wisdom literature uses the term across practical and theological settings; do not reduce it to intelligence or a promise of effortless success.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Mercy, compassion or active kindness toward someone in need. In biblical contexts it can describe God's merciful action and the mercy people are called to show.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not reduce mercy to a feeling alone or assume every occurrence carries the same covenantal or emotional nuance. Read the speaker, recipient and surrounding argument.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Compassion, tender mercy or heartfelt pity. In the New Testament it often describes God's merciful character as the ground for a transformed life and compassionate conduct.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Distinguish this noun from related words for mercy by context; do not imply compassion removes the need for justice, boundaries or wise action.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Godliness, reverent devotion or piety expressed in life. In the Pastoral Epistles it concerns a life oriented toward God rather than mere religious appearance.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not treat godliness as outward performance, social status or a guarantee of material prosperity. Read the term alongside faith, love, endurance and self-control.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Reconciliation or the restoration of a relationship. Paul uses it for the peace with God made possible through Christ and for the ministry of reconciliation entrusted to believers.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Reconciliation with God and reconciliation between people are related but not identical applications. Do not use the term to pressure victims to resume unsafe relationships without truth, repentance and protection.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Atoning sacrifice or propitiation. In 1 John it describes Christ in relation to sins and grounds assurance in God's love and the saving work of Jesus.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Christian translations and traditions differ in how they express the atonement nuance of propitiation and expiation. Explain the biblical context and do not reduce the term to a picture of a reluctant Father being persuaded to love.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: A Hebrew root with a range that includes comfort or consolation and, in other stems and contexts, relenting or changing course. The sense must be established from the form and literary setting.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not assume one English gloss fits every occurrence. The root appears in different stems and contexts; avoid making simplistic claims about God changing or not changing without examining the passage.
entries.morphologyStatus: Root-level study only; individual stems and verse forms must be parsed before assigning a specific grammatical sense.

entries.contextualGloss: Sabbath, the appointed day of cessation and rest. The noun is related to the Hebrew verb shavat, 'to cease'; biblical uses connect Sabbath with creation, covenant identity, worship and release from ordinary labour.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The Sabbath command belongs to Israel's covenant and is interpreted differently among Christian traditions. Do not flatten the creation pattern, Exodus rationale and New Testament debates into one unqualified rule.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: To remember, call to mind or bring to remembrance. In many biblical contexts remembering is more than mental recall; it is shown through faithful action in response to a person or covenant.
entries.interpretiveCaution: Do not assume every occurrence means the same kind of action. Observe who remembers whom, what is remembered and what response follows in the narrative or poem.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: To dwell, settle or reside. It appears in tabernacle and presence contexts, describing God's dwelling among His people and ordinary habitation.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The later Jewish term 'Shekinah' is related to this root but is not itself the Hebrew Bible's standard noun for God's presence. Keep the biblical verb and later theological vocabulary distinct.
entries.morphologyStatus: Lexeme-level study only; no verse-specific inflection or parsing is asserted.

entries.contextualGloss: Shield. It is used literally and metaphorically for protection, often describing God as the defender and refuge of His people.
entries.interpretiveCaution: The shield metaphor expresses trust in God's protection but is not a promise that believers will never experience physical harm. Read each poetic or covenant context carefully.
